final_proof:
For each positive integer \(n\), let
\[
\delta_n(x)=\frac{n}{\pi}\frac{1}{1+n^2x^2}.
\]
Each \(\delta_n\) is nonnegative and integrable. With the substitution \(u=nx\), we obtain
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,dx
=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{du}{1+u^2}
=\frac1\pi\bigl[\arctan u\bigr]_{-\infty}^{\infty}=1.
\]
Moreover, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the mass outside \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\) tends to zero. Indeed,
\[
\int_{|x|\geq\varepsilon}\delta_n(x)\,dx
=\frac1\pi\int_{|u|\geq n\varepsilon}\frac{du}{1+u^2}
\leq \frac{2}{\pi}\int_{n\varepsilon}^{\infty}\frac{du}{u^2}
=\frac{2}{\pi n\varepsilon}\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Thus the kernels have unit mass and concentrate at the origin, as required of a delta sequence.

It remains to verify the asserted distributional limit directly. Let \(\phi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\). After the same substitution,
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx
=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\phi(u/n)}{1+u^2}\,du.
\]
For every fixed \(u\in\mathbb R\), continuity of \(\phi\) at zero gives \(\phi(u/n)\to\phi(0)\). Also, because \(\phi\) is compactly supported and continuous, it is bounded, and for every \(n\) and \(u\),
\[
\left|\frac{\phi(u/n)}{1+u^2}\right|\leq\frac{\|\phi\|_\infty}{1+u^2}.
\]
The function on the right is integrable over \(\mathbb R\). Hence the dominated convergence theorem yields
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx
=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\phi(0)}{1+u^2}\,du
=\phi(0).
\]
By definition, the Dirac distribution \(\delta\) acts on test functions by \(\delta(\phi)=\phi(0)\). Therefore \(\langle\delta_n,\phi\rangle\to\langle\delta,\phi\rangle\) for every \(\phi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)\), which is precisely \(\delta_n\to\delta\) in \(\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)\).
